source: Marqu - The Hebrew Gospel of Mark v1.2

verses.translation: And the Pesach{H6453} was near{H7138}, and the day{H3117} of the unleavened-bread{H4682}, about two{H8147} days{H3117} away, and the chief{H8269} priests{H3548} and the Torah-scholars were endeavoring how they might seize{H8610} Yeshua{H3442} by deceit{H8267} and put him to death{H4191}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses הפסח ויום המצה (ha-Pesach ve-yom ha-Matsah — 'the Pesach and the day of the unleavened-bread', H6453+H4682) — preserving the DISTINCT Torah observances: the Pesach sacrifice (Ex 12:21,27) on the 14th of Nisan and the Festival of Matsot (Ex 12:17-20, Lev 23:6) beginning the 15th. Greek τὸ πάσχα καὶ τὰ ἄζυμα ('the Passover and the unleavened') uses pluralized Greek abstractions. The Hebrew preserves the precise liturgical calendar structure.

Uses מאותתים מהדת (me'ot'tim me-ha-dat — 'scholars/signers of the law') — a distinctly Sephardic Hebrew compound term for those who authenticate legal tradition. Greek γραμματεῖς ('scribes') is a single Greek word. No back-translator would produce this unusual two-word compound.
translation_notes: מאותתים (me'ot'tim) appears to derive from אות ('sign/letter') — those who deal with the signs/letters of the Torah, i.e., Torah scholars. This term recurs throughout the Hebrew Mark.

verses.translation: But they said{H559}: Indeed{H403}, we shall not do{H6213} it on the feast{H2282} day{H3117}, lest the people{H5971} revolt{H6965}.

And as he was in the house{H1004} of Shimon{H8095} the leper{H6879} in Beit Anya{H1042}, and sitting{H3427} at the table{H7979}, a woman{H802} came{H935} with an alabaster capsule full{H4392} of anointing{H4888} of costly spikenard{H5373}, and she broke{H7665} it and poured{H8210} the anointing{H4888} upon his head{H7218}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses משיחה (meshichah — 'anointing/anointing-oil', H4888) — the SAME root as משיח (mashiach — 'anointed one/messiah'). The woman performs a MESSIANIC ANOINTING on Yeshua's head. Greek μύρον ('perfume/ointment') lacks this theological resonance. A Hebrew reader instantly connects this act to royal anointing (1 Sam 10:1, 16:13; 1 Kgs 1:39). A back-translator from Greek μύρον would use שמן (shemen — 'oil') or בשם (bosem — 'perfume'), not the messianic anointing term.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: קאפסא אלבשטרי ('capsule of alabaster'). Greek: ἀλάβαστρον μύρου ('alabaster jar of ointment'). Hebrew uses a Romance loanword (capsa) for the vessel.
translation_notes: קאפסא (qafsa) is a loanword from Latin capsa ('box/case'). מרגלי (margali) is from Latin margarita/pearl, used here to mean 'precious/costly.' Both are markers of Sephardic Hebrew vocabulary.

verses.translation: And there were others there who were angry{H3707} among themselves: Why{H4100} was this waste{H6} made of the anointing{H4888}?

one_way_hebrew: Uses האבדה (ha-avedah — 'the loss/waste', H6 from אבד) — the specific Hebrew legal term for lost property (Ex 22:8, Deut 22:3). Greek ἀπώλεια ('destruction/waste') is broader. The Hebrew frames the complaint in property-law terms — the anointing is 'lost property' that should have been recovered for the poor.

verses.translation: For we could have sold{H4376} it for more than three{H7969} hundred{H3967} peshitin and given{H5414} it to the poor{H6041}. And they complained against her.

one_way_hebrew: Uses פשיטין (peshitin) — a post-biblical Hebrew/Aramaic monetary unit meaning 'small coins/pennies.' Greek δηναρίων ('denarii') is the Roman monetary unit. A back-translator from Greek would transliterate as דינרין. The Hebrew uses a Semitic monetary term, not a Roman one.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'peshitin' (Semitic coins). Greek: 'denarii' (Roman coins). Different monetary systems.

verses.translation: And Yeshua{H3442} said{H559} to them: Do not seize{H8610} her! Why{H4100} are you grieved{H6087}? Know{H3045} that she has wrought{H6466} a good{H2896} work{H6468}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses פעלה פעולה טובה (pa'alah pe'ulah tovah — 'she wrought a good work', H6466+H6468) — a cognate accusative construction (verb and noun from the same root). Greek καλὸν ἔργον εἰργάσατο ('she worked a good work') also has a cognate accusative. Both traditions preserve the rhetorical figure, but the Hebrew root פעל specifically means labor/wages (Lev 19:13, Deut 32:4, Isa 49:4) — connecting the woman's act to divinely-worthy labor.

verses.translation: For the poor{H6041} you shall have{H1961} forever{H5769}, and when you desire{H2654} you may do good for them, but me you shall not have{H1961} forever{H5769}.

translation_notes: Echoes Deuteronomy 15:11: כִּי לֹא יֶחְדַּל אֶבְיוֹן מִקֶּרֶב הָאָרֶץ — 'For the poor shall never cease from the midst of the land.'

verses.translation: For from what she had{H1961}, she served{H5647} me.

one_way_hebrew: Uses עבדה (avdah — 'she served', H5647) where Greek has ἔσχεν ἐποίησεν ('she has done'). The Hebrew frames the anointing as SERVICE — the same verb used for serving God (Ex 3:12, Josh 24:15) and priestly service (Num 3:7-8). The woman SERVED Yeshua in a priestly/liturgical sense. Greek merely says she 'did' something.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'she served me' (priestly/liturgical). Greek: 'she has done what she could' (practical). Different framing.

verses.translation: I say{H559} that wherever{H4725} this good-news{H1309} shall be told{H5046}, it shall be said{H559} that she did{H6213} this in my memorial{H2146}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses בזכרוני (be-zikhroni — 'in my memorial', H2146 from זכר) — the word used for memorial offerings and remembrance rituals in the Torah (Lev 2:2,9,16 — the אזכרה, memorial portion of the grain offering). Greek εἰς μνημόσυνον αὐτῆς ('as a memorial of HER'). Hebrew: 'in MY memorial' — the act memorializes Yeshua. Greek: 'as a memorial of HER' — the act memorializes the woman. The possessive pronoun differs, and the Hebrew connects to the Torah's memorial-offering vocabulary.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'in MY memorial' (בזכרוני — Yeshua is memorialized). Greek: 'as a memorial of HER' (εἰς μνημόσυνον αὐτῆς — the woman is memorialized). Different referent.

verses.translation: And Yehudah{H3063} Ashkeriot, one{H259} of the twelve{H8147}{H6240} disciples, went{H1980} to the chief priests{H3548} to deliver{H4560} him to them.

one_way_hebrew: Uses אשקריות (Ashkeriot) — preserving a Semitic form. Greek Ἰσκαριώτης (Iscariot) is debated: from איש קריות ('man of Kerioth') or from שקריא ('liar/false one'). The Hebrew form אשקריות may derive from שקר ('deceit') — making it a descriptive epithet ('the deceitful one') rather than a geographic surname.

verses.translation: And when they heard{H8085}, they were very{H3966} glad{H8056} and vowed{H5087} to give{H5414} him money{H3701}, and he sought opportunity how he might deliver{H4560} him.

one_way_hebrew: Uses נדרו (nadru — 'vowed', H5087 from נדר) — a religious vow, the same word for vows to God (Num 6:2, 21:2, 30:3; Judg 11:30). Greek ἐπηγγείλαντο ('promised') is a secular promise. The Hebrew frames the payment as a SACRED VOW — the priests make a religious commitment to pay for the betrayal. A back-translator from Greek 'promise' would use הבטיחו, not the religious vow term.

Uses מעות (ma'ot — 'coins/money', H3701 related to silver) — a post-biblical but Semitic monetary term. Greek ἀργύριον ('silver'). Both point to silver, but the Hebrew uses the common Jewish term for small coins.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'vowed' (religious). Greek: 'promised' (secular). Different nature of commitment.

verses.translation: And the first{H7223} day{H3117} of the bread{H6595} of the unleavened{H4682}, when they make{H6213} the Pesach{H6453}, his disciples said{H559} to him: Where do you desire{H2654} that we go{H1980} and prepare{H3559} for you the Pesach{H6453} to eat{H398}?

one_way_hebrew: Uses פת המצה (pat ha-matsah — 'bread of the unleavened', H6595+H4682). Greek: τῶν ἀζύμων ('of the unleavened'). The Hebrew adds פת ('bread/morsel'), specifying the physical food item, not just the abstract quality of unleavenedness. This is how a Hebrew speaker naturally refers to matzah — 'the bread of the unleavened.'
textual_notes: Exodus 12:8: וְאָכְלוּ אֶת הַבָּשָׂר... עַל מַצּוֹת — 'And they shall eat the flesh... with unleavened bread.' The Hebrew Mark naturally uses Torah Pesach vocabulary.

verses.translation: And he sent{H7971} two{H8147} of the disciples and said{H559} to them: Go{H1980} to the city{H5892} and you shall meet{H6298} a man{H120} carrying{H5375} a jar{H2789} of water{H4325}; follow him.

translation_notes: חבית (chavit — 'jar/barrel', H2789) — used in 1 Kings 17:12,14,16 for the widow of Zarephath's jar of oil. The same vessel-word.

verses.translation: And wherever he enters{H935}, say{H559} to the master{H113} of the house{H1004}: The Rabbi{H7227} says{H559}, Where{H346} is my house{H1004} where I shall eat{H398} the Pesach{H6453} with my disciples?

one_way_hebrew: Uses ביתי (beiti — 'MY house'). Greek has τὸ κατάλυμά μου ('my guest-room/lodging'). Hebrew: Yeshua calls it 'my house'; Greek: Yeshua calls it 'my guest room.' The Hebrew claim is far bolder — ownership vs. temporary lodging. A back-translator from Greek 'lodging' would use מלוני or אכסניא, not ביתי ('my house').
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'my house' (ביתי — ownership). Greek: 'my guest room' (τὸ κατάλυμα — temporary lodging). Different claim.

verses.translation: And he shall show{H7200} you a great{H1419} house{H1004} for eating{H398}, and there prepare{H3559} it, and go{H1980}.

greek_deviations: Greek adds ἐστρωμένον ἕτοιμον ('spread out, ready/furnished'). Hebrew has only 'a great house for eating' — no mention of furnishing.

verses.translation: And his disciples went{H1980} and came{H935} to the city{H5892} and found{H4672} as Yeshua{H3442} had said{H559} to them, and they prepared{H3559} the Pesach{H6453}.
And when it was evening{H6153}, Yeshua{H3442} came{H935} with the twelve{H8147}{H6240} disciples.
And while they were sitting{H3427}, Yeshua{H3442} said{H559} to them: Truth{H571} I say{H559} to you, that one{H259} of you who eats{H398} with me shall betray{H898} me.

one_way_hebrew: Uses יבגדני (yivgedeni — 'shall betray me', H898 from בגד) — the OT term for treacherous dealing and covenant violation (Jer 3:20, 12:1; Isa 24:16, 33:1; Mal 2:10-16). Greek παραδώσει με ('shall deliver me') is a neutral legal term. Hebrew: covenant TREACHERY; Greek: legal DELIVERY. A back-translator from Greek would use ימסרני ('shall deliver me'), not the covenant-betrayal term.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'shall betray me' (בגד — covenant treachery). Greek: 'shall deliver me' (παραδίδωμι — hand over). Different moral framing.
textual_notes: Psalm 41:10 (9 in English): גַּם אִישׁ שְׁלוֹמִי אֲשֶׁר בָּטַחְתִּי בוֹ אוֹכֵל לַחְמִי הִגְדִּיל עָלַי עָקֵב — 'Even my close friend whom I trusted, who ate my bread, has lifted his heel against me.' The 'one who eats with me' echoes this psalm of betrayal.

verses.translation: And they were grieved{H6087} and each{H376} one began to say{H559}: Master{H113}, is it I{H589}?

one_way_hebrew: Uses אדון (adon — 'master/lord', H113). Greek: μήτι ἐγώ ('surely not I?'). The Hebrew adds the ADDRESS 'Master' before the question, absent from the Greek. The disciples' grief is expressed with the deference of servants before their lord.
greek_deviations: Hebrew includes 'Master' (אדון) as a form of address. Greek has only the question 'surely not I?'

verses.translation: And he said{H559} to them: One{H259} of the twelve{H8147}{H6240} who dips{H7971} his hand{H3027} with me in the bowl{H7086}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses קערה (qe'arah — 'bowl/dish', H7086) — the same word used for the Tabernacle's golden bowls (Num 7:13,19,25,31 etc. — the offering bowls of the twelve tribal leaders). Greek τρύβλιον ('dish/bowl') is a common table vessel. The Pesach dish is described with Tabernacle vocabulary.

verses.translation: The Son{H1121} of God{H433} goes{H1980} as the prophecy{H5016} says{H559}; but woe{H1945} to the man{H120} by{H5668} whom the Son{H1121} of the Virgin{H1330} shall be betrayed{H898} — it were a good{H2896} thing{H1697} for that man{H376} if he had not been born{H3205}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses BOTH בן האלוה (ben ha-Eloah — 'Son of God') AND בן הבתולה (ben ha-Betulah — 'Son of the Virgin', H1330) IN THE SAME VERSE. Greek has ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου ('the Son of Man') for both references. This is the most dramatic divergence in the entire Hebrew Mark. The Hebrew author uses TWO DISTINCT Christological titles — one divine (Son of God) and one incarnational (Son of the Virgin) — where the Greek uses a single title (Son of Man) twice. No back-translator from Greek 'Son of Man' would produce EITHER 'Son of God' OR 'Son of the Virgin,' let alone both.

בן הבתולה (ben ha-Betulah — 'Son of the Virgin') echoes Isaiah 7:14: הִנֵּה הָעַלְמָה הָרָה — 'Behold, the young woman/virgin is with child.' The Hebrew Gospels use בתולה (betulah — 'virgin', the stronger virginity term) rather than Isaiah's עלמה (almah — 'young woman'). This title 'Son of the Virgin' has no Greek equivalent and appears to be a uniquely Hebrew Christological formula.
greek_deviations: Hebrew first reference: 'Son of God' (בן האלוה). Greek: 'Son of Man.' Different title entirely.
Hebrew second reference: 'Son of the Virgin' (בן הבתולה). Greek: 'Son of Man.' No Greek equivalent for this title.
translation_notes: 'Son of the Virgin' is translated literally to preserve this unique Hebrew Christological title. It combines incarnational theology (born of a virgin) with the messianic 'Son of' formula.
textual_notes: The dual-title structure 'Son of God... Son of the Virgin' encapsulates a two-nature Christology: divine origin (Son of God) and human entry (Son of the Virgin). This is theologically sophisticated in a way that 'Son of Man' (used twice in Greek) is not.

verses.translation: And as they were eating{H398}, he took{H3947} the bread{H6595} and said{H559}: This is my heart{H3820}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses לבי (libi — 'my heart', H3820). Greek has τοῦτό ἐστι τὸ σῶμά μου ('this is my body'). MASSIVE divergence. Hebrew: 'This is my HEART.' Greek: 'This is my BODY.' A back-translator from Greek 'body' would write גופי (gufi) or בשרי (besari — 'my flesh'), NEVER לבי ('my heart'). The Hebrew makes the bread a symbol of Yeshua's INNER SELF — his will, love, and intent — rather than his physical body. This reframes the entire Last Supper theology.

The Hebrew לב (lev — 'heart') in the OT is the seat of thought, will, and moral decision (Deut 6:5 — 'love YHWH with all your heart'; 1 Kgs 3:9 — Solomon asks for a 'hearing heart'; Jer 31:33 — the Torah written on the 'heart'). Yeshua gives his disciples his HEART — his Torah-filled, God-directed inner self.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'my heart' (לבי). Greek: 'my body' (σῶμα). Irreconcilable divergence — inner self vs. physical form.
translation_notes: 'Heart' for libi — this must NOT be softened to 'body' or 'self.' The Hebrew word is unambiguously לב (heart), the OT seat of cognition and will.
textual_notes: Jeremiah 31:33: 'I will put my Torah in their inner parts, and write it on their HEART (לב).' Yeshua giving his 'heart' at Pesach echoes the New Covenant promise of Torah internalized.

verses.translation: And he took{H3947} the cup{H1375} and gave thanks and gave{H5414} it to them, and they drank{H8354} from it.

one_way_hebrew: Uses גביע (gavia — 'cup/goblet', H1375) — the specific word for Joseph's silver divination cup (Gen 44:2,12,16,17) and the flower-cups of the Menorah (Ex 25:31,33,34). This is not the common כוס (kos — 'cup'). Greek ποτήριον is a generic drinking vessel. The Hebrew uses the ornamental, ceremonial cup-word.
translation_notes: חנות (chanot — 'thanks/favor') — from חן (chen — grace). The Hebrew blessing is an act of GRACE-giving, not merely 'giving thanks' (Greek εὐχαριστήσας).

verses.translation: And he said{H559} to them: This is my blood{H1818} which for the sake of many{H7227} shall be poured out{H8210}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses ישפך (yishafekh — 'shall be poured out', H8210 from שפך) — the specific verb for the pouring of blood at the altar base (Lev 4:7,18,25,30,34 — the sin offering blood). Greek ἐκχυνόμενον ('being poured out') is also sacrificial but the Hebrew שפך specifically echoes the Levitical altar protocol. The Pesach cup IS the altar.

Hebrew OMITS the covenant formula. Greek has τοῦτό ἐστι τὸ αἷμά μου τῆς καινῆς διαθήκης ('this is my blood of the NEW COVENANT'). The Hebrew has simply 'my blood which for many shall be poured out' — no mention of covenant (ברית), new or old. This is a MAJOR omission that a back-translator would not produce.
greek_deviations: Hebrew OMITS 'of the new covenant' (τῆς καινῆς διαθήκης). The Hebrew gives the blood significance without invoking covenant language.

verses.translation: Truth{H571} I say{H559} to you, that I shall not drink of the wine{H3196} of the vine{H1612} until I drink{H8354} it new{H2319} in the kingdom{H4438} of my Father{H1}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses מלכות אבי (malkhut avi — 'kingdom of my Father'). Greek: ἐν τῇ βασιλείᾳ τοῦ θεοῦ ('in the kingdom of GOD'). Hebrew: 'my Father'; Greek: 'God.' The Hebrew preserves the intimate filial address; the Greek uses the formal divine title.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'kingdom of my Father.' Greek: 'kingdom of God.' Different divine reference.

verses.translation: And when they had given thanks, they went out{H3318} to the Mount{H2022} of Olives{H2132}.

greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'they gave thanks' (plural — all participants). Greek: ὑμνήσαντες ('having sung a hymn'). Hebrew: thanksgiving; Greek: hymn-singing. Different worship acts.
translation_notes: The Pesach Hallel (Psalms 113-118) was traditionally sung at the conclusion of the seder. Greek 'hymn' likely refers to this. Hebrew 'thanks' may be a more general description.

verses.translation: And Yeshua{H3442} said{H559} to them: All{H3605} of you shall stumble{H3782} on account of me this night{H3915}, for it is written{H3789}: I shall strike{H5221} the shepherd{H7462} and the flock{H6629} shall scatter{H6327}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses אני אכה (ani akeh — 'I shall strike', first person). This quotes Zechariah 13:7 where the MT has הַךְ (hakh — imperative 'strike!') addressed to the sword: 'Sword, awake against my shepherd... strike the shepherd.' The Hebrew Gospel changes the imperative to FIRST PERSON — 'I shall strike' — making GOD the direct agent. Greek πατάξω ('I will strike') also has first person. Both traditions agree against the MT imperative, but the Hebrew's אכה is a deliberate theological choice — God strikes his own shepherd.

Uses נכשלים (nikhshalim — 'stumbling', H3782 from כשל) — the word for spiritual stumbling and falling (Isa 8:15, 28:13, 31:3; Jer 6:21; Hos 4:5, 5:5, 14:2). Greek σκανδαλισθήσεσθε ('scandalized/offended'). Hebrew: they will STUMBLE (lose their footing); Greek: they will be SCANDALIZED (morally offended). A back-translator from Greek would use תתקלקלו or תתבלבלו.
textual_notes: Zechariah 13:7 MT: הַךְ אֶת הָרֹעֶה וּתְפוּצֶיןָ הַצֹּאן — 'Strike the shepherd, and the flock shall be scattered.' Both Hebrew Mark and Greek change the MT's imperative to first person, suggesting a shared pre-textual tradition.

verses.translation: Indeed{H403}, after I return{H7725} alive{H2416}, I shall be{H1961} with you in the Galil{H1551}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses שאחזור חי (she-achzor chai — 'after I return alive', H7725+H2416). Greek: μετὰ τὸ ἐγερθῆναί με ('after I am raised/resurrected'). Hebrew says 'RETURN ALIVE' — implying departure and return, not death and resurrection per se. Greek says 'BE RAISED' — passive, implying God raises him. These are fundamentally different resurrection concepts. The Hebrew frames it as COMING BACK to life (active return); the Greek frames it as BEING RAISED from death (passive divine act).
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'after I return alive' (active — Yeshua returns). Greek: 'after I am raised' (passive — God raises him). Different agency.

verses.translation: And Kefa{H3710} said{H559}: Even if all{H3605} stumble{H3782}, I shall not.

And Yeshua{H3442} said{H559} to him: Truth{H571} I say{H559} to you, in this night{H3915}, before{H6924} the rooster{H8500} calls{H7121} twice{H8147}, you shall deny{H3584} me three{H7969} times{H6471}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses כופר (kofer — 'denying', H3584 from כפר) — the specific verb for denying God and denying truth (Josh 24:27, Job 8:18, 31:28; Prov 30:9). Greek ἀπαρνήσῃ ('deny/disown') is also strong. But the Hebrew כפר in the denial sense carries the specific weight of denying what one knows to be true — a conscious, deliberate falsehood before God.

verses.translation: And he yet spoke{H1696} further, saying{H559}: If I am compelled to die{H4191} with you, I shall not deny{H3584} you. And so said{H559} all{H3605} the others.
And they came{H935} to a field{H7704} whose name{H8034} is Gat Shemani{H1660}, and he said{H559} to his disciples: Sit{H3427} here until I finish praying{H6419}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses גת שמני (Gat Shemani — 'oil-press', H1660+H8081). גת (gat) means 'press/winepress' (Judg 6:11, Joel 4:13, Neh 13:15) and שמני (shemani) means 'of oil/oily' (from שמן, shemen — 'oil'). The Hebrew preserves the transparent meaning: this is an OIL-PRESS location. Greek Γεθσημανῆ is an opaque transliteration that conveys no meaning to Greek readers. A back-translator from Greek would just transliterate back. Only the Hebrew reveals the profound irony: Yeshua, the 'Anointed One' (מָשִׁיחַ, from שמן 'oil'), is PRESSED at the oil-press.

Calls the location a שדה (sadeh — 'field', H7704). Greek has χωρίον ('place/plot of ground'). Hebrew specifically says it is agricultural land — a field with an oil-press, not merely a 'garden' (κῆπος, as John calls it).
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'a field whose name is Gat Shemani.' Greek: 'a place named Gethsemane.' Hebrew reveals the meaning; Greek obscures it.
translation_notes: 'Gat Shemani' is left untranslated as a place name but its meaning ('oil-press') is crucial. The Anointed One (from oil) is pressed at the oil-press.

verses.translation: And he took{H3947} with him Kefa{H3710} and Ya'aqov{H3290} and Yochanan{H3110}, and he began to pray{H6419} and to be afraid{H6342}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses להתפלל ולהתפחד (le-hitpalel ve-le-hitpached — 'to pray and to be afraid'). Greek ἤρξατο ἐκθαμβεῖσθαι καὶ ἀδημονεῖν ('began to be greatly amazed and distressed'). Hebrew puts PRAYER first, then fear. Greek has amazement and distress but NO prayer at this point. The Hebrew shows Yeshua entering prayer as his FIRST response to the crisis; the Greek shows emotional reaction first.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'to pray and to be afraid.' Greek: 'to be amazed and distressed.' Hebrew includes prayer; Greek has only emotional states.

verses.translation: And he said{H559} to them: My soul{H5315} is grieved{H6087} unto death{H4194}; wait{H3176} for me here and be awake{H5782}.

one_way_hebrew: DIRECT ECHO of Psalm 42:6,12 / 43:5: מַה תִּשְׁתּוֹחֲחִי נַפְשִׁי — 'Why are you cast down, O my soul?' and Jonah 4:9: 'I am grieved unto death' (כי טוב מותי מחיי). The Hebrew נפשי עצבה עד מות uses the OT soul-grief formula.
textual_notes: Psalm 42:6 (5): מַה תִּשְׁתּוֹחֲחִי נַפְשִׁי וַתֶּהֱמִי עָלָי — 'Why are you cast down, O my soul, and why are you in turmoil within me?' Yeshua's words echo the psalmist's lament.

verses.translation: And as he withdrew{H3766} a little{H4592}, he fell{H3766} on his face{H639} to the ground{H776} and prayed{H6419} to the Name{H8034}, if it were possible{H3201}, that that hour{H8160} might pass{H5674}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses כרע באפיו ארצה (kara be-apav artsah — 'fell on his face to the ground') — the standard OT prostration formula (Gen 17:3, Num 14:5, 16:4,22, 20:6; Josh 5:14, 7:6). Greek ἔπιπτεν ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς ('fell upon the earth') is simpler. The Hebrew uses the full liturgical prostration language — face to the ground.
Uses לשם (la-Shem — 'to the Name') — praying TO the Name, again the reverential circumlocution for God.

verses.translation: And he said{H559}: Father{H1}, who is able{H3201}, remove{H7368} this death from me; yet let it not be by my will{H7522}, but by your will{H7522}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses המימה (ha-mimah — 'the death') where Greek has τὸ ποτήριον τοῦτο ('this cup'). MASSIVE divergence. Hebrew: 'remove this DEATH from me.' Greek: 'remove this CUP from me.' A back-translator from Greek 'cup' would write הכוס or הגביע, NEVER המימה ('the death'). The Hebrew Yeshua asks directly for DEATH to be removed; the Greek Yeshua asks for the symbolic CUP to pass. The Hebrew is raw and concrete; the Greek is metaphorical.

Uses רצון (ratson — 'will/desire/favor', H7522) — the OT word for divine favor and human will (Ps 40:9, 103:21, 143:10; Prov 12:2, 14:9). Greek θέλημα ('will') is adequate but ratson carries the additional nuance of DELIGHT — 'not my delight but your delight.'
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'this death' (המימה). Greek: 'this cup' (τὸ ποτήριον). Concrete vs. metaphorical.
Hebrew: 'Father, who is able' (אב שהוא היכול). Greek: 'Abba, Father' (αββα ὁ πατήρ). Hebrew attributes ABILITY to God; Greek doubles the paternal address.
translation_notes: המימה (ha-mimah) is a later Hebrew form of מיתה (mitah — 'death'), from the root מות. Not 'cup,' not 'bitterness' — the word means DEATH.

verses.translation: And he came{H935} and found{H4672} them sleeping{H3463}, and said{H559} to Kefa{H3710} and to Shimon{H8095}: Are you sleeping{H3463}? And you were not able{H3201} to be awake{H5782} with me?

one_way_hebrew: Addresses both כיפא (Kefa) and שמעון (Shimon) — using both names of the same person. Greek has only Σίμων (Simon). The Hebrew preserves BOTH the Aramaic nickname (Kefa/Rock) and the Hebrew birth name (Shimon), suggesting an author who knows him by both names.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'to Kefa and to Shimon' (both names). Greek: only 'Simon' (Σίμωνι).

verses.translation: Be awake{H5782} and pray{H6419}, that you not enter{H935} into trial{H5254}. The spirit{H7307} is willing{H3559}, but the flesh{H1320} is weak{H2470}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses חולה (choleh — 'sick/weak', H2470 from חלה) for the flesh. Greek ἀσθενής ('weak') is generic weakness. The Hebrew says the flesh is SICK — a medical/disease metaphor. The body is not merely feeble but AILING. A back-translator from Greek 'weak' would use חלש (chalash), not the sickness term חולה.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'the flesh is sick' (חולה). Greek: 'the flesh is weak' (ἀσθενής). Medical vs. generic.

verses.translation: And again he went{H1980} to pray{H6419} with that same word{H4405}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses מלה (milah — 'word', H4405) — the Aramaic/poetic Hebrew word for 'word' found in Job (4:2, 12:11, 23:5, 32:11, 33:8, 34:16, 35:4, 36:2) and Daniel. Greek τὸν αὐτὸν λόγον ('the same word/saying'). Both traditions note the repetition, but the Hebrew uses the rare/poetic term for speech, not the common דבר.

verses.translation: And when he returned{H7725}, he found{H4672} them sleeping{H3463}, for their eyes{H5869} were heavy{H3515}, and they could not answer{H6030} him.

He came{H935} again and said{H559} to them: Are you still sleeping{H3463}? It is enough{H1767}. The hour{H8160} has come{H935} that the Son{H1121} of the Virgin{H1330} shall be delivered{H4560} into the hands{H3027} of the sinners{H2400}.

one_way_hebrew: Again uses בן הבתולה (ben ha-Betulah — 'Son of the Virgin', H1121+H1330). Greek again has ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου ('Son of Man'). Second occurrence of this unique Hebrew title in this chapter, confirming it is the author's consistent choice, not a scribal error.

Uses החוטאים (ha-chot'im — 'the sinners', H2400 from חטא) — the standard OT term for those who miss the mark of Torah (Num 32:14, 1 Sam 15:18, Isa 1:28, 33:14). Greek ἁμαρτωλῶν ('sinners') is a direct semantic equivalent. Both traditions agree here.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'Son of the Virgin.' Greek: 'Son of Man.' Same divergence as v21.

verses.translation: Rise{H6965} and let us go{H1980}, for behold{H2009}, he who delivers{H4560} me is near{H7138}.

While he was yet speaking{H1696}, Yehudah{H3063} Ashkeriot came{H935}, one{H259} of the twelve{H8147}{H6240} disciples, and with him a great{H7227} crowd{H5971} with knives{H7915} and staves{H4731}, and he was sent{H7971} by the deputy{H5461} of the priests{H3548} and by the Torah-scholars and the elders{H2205} of the people{H5971}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses סכינים (sakinim — 'knives') — a post-biblical Hebrew word for cutting implements. Greek μαχαιρῶν ('swords'). Hebrew: KNIVES (domestic/butchering tools); Greek: SWORDS (military weapons). A back-translator from Greek 'swords' would use חרבות (charavot). The Hebrew suggests a hastily-armed mob with kitchen/butchering knives, not a military detachment with swords.

Uses סגן הכהנים (segan ha-kohanim — 'deputy of the priests', H5461) — the OT title for the second-in-command of the Temple hierarchy (Neh 11:11, Jer 20:1, 2 Kgs 25:18). Greek ἀρχιερέων ('chief priests') is plural and more generic. The Hebrew preserves a specific Temple administrative title.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'knives' (domestic). Greek: 'swords' (military). Different weapons.
Hebrew: 'deputy of the priests' (specific rank). Greek: 'chief priests' (general).

verses.translation: And the betrayer{H898} had given{H5414} them this sign{H226}, saying{H559}: The one whom I kiss{H5401}, he is the one; seize{H8610} him and bring him away carefully{H2451}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses בחכמה (be-chokhmah — 'with wisdom/carefully', H2451) — the OT wisdom word (Prov 1:2,7, 2:6; Ex 31:3). Greek ἀσφαλῶς ('safely/securely') is merely cautious. The Hebrew says bring him 'with wisdom' — implying cunning strategy, not just physical security.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'with wisdom' (בחכמה). Greek: 'safely' (ἀσφαλῶς). Wisdom vs. safety.

verses.translation: And immediately{H4116} when he came{H935}, he drew near{H5066} to him saying{H559}: Peace{H7965} be upon you, Rabbi{H7227}! And he kissed{H5401} him.

one_way_hebrew: Uses שלום עליך (shalom aleikha — 'peace be upon you', H7965) — the standard Hebrew greeting. Greek has χαῖρε ῥαββί ('Hail, Rabbi!'). Hebrew: a PEACE blessing; Greek: a HAIL/rejoice greeting. A back-translator from Greek χαῖρε would use ששון or שמח, not the שלום blessing.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'peace upon you' (blessing). Greek: 'hail!' (greeting). Different speech acts.

verses.translation: And they laid{H7760} hands{H3027} on him and seized{H2388} him.
And one{H259} of those who were with Yeshua{H3442} drew{H3318} the knife and struck{H5221} a servant{H5650} of the deputy{H5461} of the priests{H3548} and cut off{H3772} his ear{H241}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses וחתך (va-chatak — 'and cut off') — the Hebrew verb for cutting covenants (כרת ברית, Gen 15:18) is from this same root כרת (karat, H3772). Greek ἀφεῖλεν ('took away/cut off') is generic. The Hebrew verb for severing the ear is the COVENANT-CUTTING verb — a bitter irony at the moment of covenant betrayal.

verses.translation: And Yeshua{H3442} answered{H6030} and said{H559} to them: As though I were a thief{H1590}, you came out{H3318} with knives and staves{H4731} to seize{H8610} me.
Every{H3605} day{H3117} I was with you in the sanctuary{H4720} teaching{H3925}, and you did not seize{H8610} me. This was done{H6213} to complete{H7999} the writings{H3791}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses הכתיבות (ha-ketivot — 'the writings', from H3791 כתב) — a plural noun meaning 'written documents/scriptures.' Greek αἱ γραφαί ('the scriptures') is equivalent. The Hebrew uses a form that emphasizes the ACT of writing — these are things that were written down, documents. The focus is on the recorded, authored quality of scripture.

verses.translation: And then the disciples all{H3605} fled{H1272} and left{H5800} him.
And a certain young man{H5288}, Malbishan, who was clothed{H3847} in a single white{H3836} linen-garment{H5466}, and they seized{H8610} him.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses מלבישן (Malbishan) as a PROPER NAME. Greek has νεανίσκος τις ('a certain young man') — an anonymous figure. The Hebrew identifies this person BY NAME. If the Hebrew were a back-translation from Greek, why would the translator invent a name? The word מלביש (malbish) means 'one who clothes/dresser,' and with the suffix -ן it becomes a personal name: 'the Clothier' or 'the Well-Dressed One.' This is a Hebrew proper name that Greek readers would not recognize.

Uses סדין (sadin, H5466 — 'linen garment/sheet') — the same word from Judges 14:12-13 (Samson's riddle involving linen garments) and Proverbs 31:24 (the woman of valor who makes linen). Greek σινδόνα ('linen cloth/shroud') is a loanword FROM Semitic. The Hebrew is the original.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'Malbishan' (named individual). Greek: 'a certain young man' (anonymous). The Hebrew identifies the person; Greek does not.
translation_notes: מלבישן (Malbishan) is preserved as a proper name. It derives from the root לבש (lavash — 'to wear/clothe'), suggesting a trade name — 'the Clothier' or 'Garment-maker.'

verses.translation: And he left{H5800} the linen-garment{H5466} and fled{H1272} from them entirely{H3605} naked{H6174}.
And they led{H5090} Yeshua{H3442} to the deputy{H5461} of the priests{H3548}, and all{H3605} the priests{H3548} and the Torah-scholars and the elders{H2205} of the people{H5971} gathered{H622}.

And Kefa{H3710} followed{H1980} him from afar{H7350}, unto a hall{H1964} of the high{H1419} priest{H3548}, and was sitting{H3427} before{H6440} the fire{H784} with the servants{H8334}, warming himself.
And the high{H1419} priest{H3548} and all{H3605} the council{H6098} sought{H2664} false{H8267} witnesses{H5707}, that they might deliver{H4560} him to death{H4194}, but they found{H4672} none.

one_way_hebrew: Uses עידי שקר (edei sheqer — 'witnesses of falsehood', H5707+H8267). Greek μαρτυρίαν κατὰ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ ('testimony against Jesus'). The Hebrew explicitly labels the witnesses as FALSE from the start. The Greek is neutral — just 'testimony against.' The Hebrew narrator editorializes, exposing the judicial corruption; the Greek presents the surface procedure.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'false witnesses' (editorial judgment). Greek: 'testimony against him' (procedural description).

verses.translation: And many{H7227} false{H8267} witnesses{H5707} spoke{H559} against Yeshua{H3442}, but they did not agree{H5574}.
And some false{H8267} witnesses{H5707} stood up{H6965} against him, saying{H559}:

We heard{H8085} him saying{H559}: I shall destroy{H2040} this sanctuary{H4720} made{H6213} by hands{H3027} of men{H376}, and in three{H7969} days{H3117} another, new{H2319}, not made{H6213} by hands{H3027} of men{H376}, I shall build{H1129}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses חרש (charash — 'new/fresh') — a variant of חדש (chadash, H2319) reflecting later Hebrew pronunciation. The Hebrew testimony includes both 'made by hands' and 'NOT made by hands' — but note the Hebrew literally says 'another new one, made by hands of men, I shall build,' which may be a confused witness testimony or a textual corruption of 'NOT made by hands.'
greek_deviations: Greek explicitly has ἄλλον ἀχειροποίητον ('another, NOT made with hands'). The Hebrew text as it stands appears to say 'made by hands of men' for both, which may reflect the deliberate confusion of false testimony.

verses.translation: And their testimony{H5715} did not agree.
And the high{H1419} priest{H3548} stood up{H6965} among them and asked{H7592} Yeshua{H3442}, saying{H559}: Do you not count{H4487} the accusations that these lay against you?

And Yeshua{H3442} was silent{H2790} and answered{H6030} not a word{H1697}. And again the high{H1419} priest{H3548} asked{H7592} him, saying{H559}: Are you the Anointed{H4899}, the Son{H1121} of the blessed{H1288} Name{H8034}?

one_way_hebrew: Uses השם הברוך (ha-Shem ha-Barukh — 'the blessed Name') — a characteristically Jewish reverential circumlocution for God. Greek τοῦ εὐλογητοῦ ('the Blessed One') — a divine epithet without 'Name.' The Hebrew adds השם ('the Name') to the 'blessed' epithet, reflecting Jewish liturgical practice: God is referred to as 'the Name' and 'the Blessed Name' in prayer. A back-translator from Greek 'the Blessed' would write הברוך alone, without adding השם.
Echoes Isaiah 53:7: כַּשֶּׂה לַטֶּבַח יוּבָל... וְלֹא יִפְתַּח פִּיו — 'Like a lamb led to slaughter... he did not open his mouth.' Yeshua's silence fulfills the suffering servant prophecy.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'Son of the blessed Name' (השם הברוך). Greek: 'Son of the Blessed' (τοῦ εὐλογητοῦ). Hebrew adds 'Name.'

verses.translation: And Yeshua{H3442} said{H559} to them: I am he{H1931}. And you shall see{H7200} the Son{H1121} of God{H433} at the right hand{H3225} of the power{H3581} of God{H410}, coming{H935} in the clouds{H5645} of the heavens{H8064}.

one_way_hebrew: Again uses בן האלוה (ben ha-Eloah — 'Son of God') where Greek has τὸν υἱὸν τοῦ ἀνθρώπου ('Son of Man'). Before the highest Jewish court, Yeshua identifies himself as 'Son of God' in the Hebrew — a far more explosive claim than 'Son of Man.'

Uses בעבי השמים (be-avei ha-shamayim — 'in the clouds/thick clouds of the heavens', H5645). Greek ἐπὶ τῶν νεφελῶν ('upon the clouds'). Hebrew עב (av — 'thick cloud') is the specific word for the cloud of God's presence (1 Kgs 18:44, Ps 18:12, 68:34). These are THEOPHANY clouds, not weather clouds.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'Son of God.' Greek: 'Son of Man.' Same divergence as Mark 13:26.
Hebrew: 'in the thick-clouds of heaven' (theophany). Greek: 'upon the clouds of heaven' (generic).
textual_notes: Psalm 110:1: נְאֻם יְהוָה לַאדֹנִי שֵׁב לִימִינִי — 'YHWH declares to my lord: Sit at my right hand.' Daniel 7:13: עִם עֲנָנֵי שְׁמַיָּא — 'with the clouds of heaven.' Yeshua combines both passages.

verses.translation: And the high{H1419} priest{H3548} tore{H7167} his garments{H899} and said{H559} to them: Do you ask{H7592} after this? And you desire{H3700} witnesses{H5707}?

one_way_hebrew: Uses כוספים (kosfim — 'yearning/desiring', H3700 from כסף) — the verb for intense longing and desire (Gen 31:30, Ps 17:12, 84:3). Greek χρείαν ἔχετε ('you have need'). Hebrew: do you still YEARN for witnesses? Greek: do you still NEED witnesses? The Hebrew is more emotionally charged — the desire for evidence after such a statement is absurd.
textual_notes: The high priest's tearing of garments is forbidden by Leviticus 21:10 for the high priest. The Hebrew narrates this violation of Torah without comment.

verses.translation: You have heard{H8085} the blasphemy{H7043}! What{H4100} is your opinion{H1847}? And they all{H3605} condemned{H6064} him.

one_way_hebrew: Uses קללה (qelalah — 'curse/blasphemy', H7043 from קלל) — the OT term for cursing God (Lev 24:11,14,23) and cursing a ruler (Ex 22:27). Greek βλασφημίαν ('blasphemy') is a Greek concept. The Hebrew uses the specific Levitical curse-word, invoking the death penalty of Leviticus 24:16.

verses.translation: And they spat{H7556} upon him and covered{H3680} his face{H6440} and struck{H5221} him on the neck{H6677}, and striking him they said{H559}: Prophesy{H5012}! Who [struck you]? And the servants{H8334} gave{H5414} him blows.

one_way_hebrew: Uses תפוחים (tapuchim — 'blows', lit. 'swellings/apples') — an unusual Hebrew term for physical strikes. Greek ῥαπίσμασιν ἔλαβον ('received slaps'). The Hebrew word can mean both 'apples' (Song 2:5) and 'swollen blows.' This ambiguity is impossible in Greek and marks a native Hebrew idiom.

verses.translation: And while Kefa{H3710} was in one side of the hall{H1964}, a maidservant{H8198} of the high{H1419} priest{H3548} came{H935}.
And when she saw{H7200} Kefa{H3710} lacing his sandal{H5275}, she looked at him{H5027} and said{H559}: And you were with Yeshua{H3442} of Natseret{H5341}.

one_way_hebrew: UNIQUE DETAIL: שנועל נעלו (she-no'el na'alo — 'lacing his sandal'). This specific physical detail — Peter adjusting his shoe — is ABSENT from the Greek entirely. Greek says only 'warming himself' (θερμαινόμενον). A back-translator would not invent 'lacing his sandal.' This is a vivid eyewitness detail preserved only in the Hebrew.
greek_deviations: Hebrew adds 'lacing his sandal' — unique physical detail absent from Greek.

verses.translation: And he denied{H3584}, saying: I do not know{H3045} and I do not recognize{H5234} what you are saying{H559}. And he went outside{H2351} and stood{H5975} before the hall{H1964}, and the rooster called{H7121}.
And immediately{H4116} a maidservant{H8198} saw{H7200} him and began{H2490} to say{H559} to those standing around{H5439} her: This one is of them.
And he again denied{H3584}. And shortly after, again one of those who sat{H3427} there said{H559} to Kefa{H3710}: Truly{H571} you are of them, for truly{H571} you are a Galilean{H1551}.

greek_deviations: Greek adds 'your speech matches' (ἡ λαλιά σου ὁμοιάζει) — identifying the Galilean accent. Hebrew identifies him as 'Galilean' without specifying how he was recognized.

verses.translation: And he began to curse{H7043} and to swear{H7650} that he does not know{H3045} the man{H376} she speaks of.

And immediately{H4116} the rooster called{H7121} again, and Kefa{H3710} remembered{H2142} the word{H1697} that Yeshua{H3442} had said{H559} to him, that before the rooster calls{H7121} twice{H8147}, he would deny{H3584} him three{H7969} times{H6471}. And he began{H2490} to weep{H1058}.

greek_deviations: Greek adds ἐπιβαλὼν ἔκλαιεν ('having thrown himself on, he wept') — a physical gesture. Hebrew simply says 'he began to weep.' The Greek adds the prostration; the Hebrew focuses on the tears.

chapter_notes.summary: Mark 14 in Hebrew presents the Passion narrative with several extraordinary divergences from the Greek TR. The most striking one-way markers include: (1) בן האלוה / בן הבתולה (vv21,41,62) — 'Son of God' and 'Son of the Virgin' where Greek consistently has 'Son of Man,' representing an entirely different Christological vocabulary; (2) לבי (v22) — 'This is my HEART' at the Last Supper where Greek has 'This is my BODY,' reframing the eucharistic theology from physicality to interiority; (3) המימה (v36) — 'remove this DEATH from me' where Greek has 'remove this CUP,' replacing metaphor with raw directness; (4) גת שמני (v32) — 'oil-press,' preserving the transparent Hebrew meaning lost in the Greek transliteration; (5) מלבישן (v51) — a PROPER NAME for the anonymous young man, an inexplicable detail if translated from Greek; (6) סכינים (vv43,48) — 'knives' where Greek has 'swords,' domestic weapons vs. military ones; (7) שלום עליך (v45) — the peace blessing vs. Greek 'Hail!'; (8) בזכרוני (v9) — 'in MY memorial' vs. Greek 'as a memorial of HER'; (9) שאחזור חי (v28) — 'after I return alive' vs. Greek 'after I am raised.' The Hebrew omits the 'new covenant' formula (v24), names Barabbas 'Bar-Aven' (Ch15:7), and uses consistent reverential circumlocutions (השם, השם הברוך). These cannot be explained as back-translation from Greek.
